papers.abstract: An ideal (language) model must continually update its knowledge. Existing work largely focuses on making these updates efficient after training. We investigate how the organization of time-varying knowledge during pre-training shapes the efficiency of subsequent updates. Models trained on chronologically ordered knowledge specialize in the most recently encountered knowledge; we call them specialists. In contrast, models trained on the same knowledge in randomly shuffled order perform well across all represented time periods; we call them generalists. Surprisingly, specialists require far fewer update steps than generalists to acquire new knowledge. To explain this advantage, we derive a law from first principles that relates update cost to the model's optimization dynamics and that closely predicts empirical results. Guided by these findings, we design a strategy for organizing pre-training data that preserves stable historical knowledge while enabling efficient updates to current knowledge. We also show that the benefits of temporal knowledge organization extend to real-world pre-trained models and existing knowledge update tools, and generalize to other knowledge orderings. Project page: https://horizon-lab.org/specialist/
bullets: Chronological training makes models specialize in recently encountered knowledge, whereas shuffled training produces broader generalists.
Specialists need far fewer update steps to learn new knowledge than generalists.
The paper derives a first-principles law linking update cost to optimization dynamics and predicting empirical behavior.
A data-ordering strategy preserves stable historical knowledge while facilitating updates to current knowledge.
The findings extend to real-world pre-trained models, existing knowledge-editing tools, and other knowledge orderings.
papers.selection_reason: Studies how pre-training knowledge organization affects update efficiency, relevant to continual learning and LLM training.
papers.title: Specialists Learn Faster: Knowledge Organization in Pre-training Shapes Knowledge Update Efficiency
papers.tldr: Organizing pre-training knowledge chronologically creates specialists that update substantially more efficiently than generalists while preserving historical knowledge.

papers.abstract: Continuous diffusion language models (CDLMs) promise to bring the benefits of continuous flow modelling to language, including accelerated sampling and controllable generation. The field has grown rapidly, and the capabilities of CDLMs have begun to rival those of discrete diffusion. Yet, unlike for continuous modalities such as images or videos, our grasp of the levers that matter when training CDLMs remains limited. In this work, we focus on two of these levers, namely self-conditioning and embedding geometry, and shed light on some of the mechanisms behind them, which in turn suggest cheaper and more effective designs. We begin by showing that self-conditioning corrects a train/inference mismatch by exposing the model to inference-like states that are otherwise rare during training. These gains can be recovered without an extra forward pass by a two-level interpolant, coined $\mathrm{DoubleCat}$, which improves TinyGSM accuracy more than threefold. Self-conditioning also aids in recognising tokens dominated by large-norm Gaussians$\unicode{x2013}$an issue known as token identifiability. To address it directly, we introduce discrete reveals to $\mathrm{DoubleCat}$, yielding $\mathrm{SemiCat}$, which achieves discrete diffusion-level performance on TinyGSM, reaching $49.94\%$ with standard training hyperparameters and a tuned sampler. At the $1.7$B scale, $\mathrm{SemiCat}$ outperforms discrete diffusion on four of six likelihood-based evaluations, and surpasses one-hot flows on unconditional generation. On embedded spaces, we find that cross-entropy drives embeddings towards a geometry whose decoding error rate closely matches the one-hot one. We briefly explore a range of further options, such as hybrid corruption processes and noise schedules, including asynchronous ones. We believe this exploration can help the community better understand and advance the design space of CDLMs.
bullets: Studies self-conditioning and embedding geometry as important but underexplored CDLM design levers.
Explains self-conditioning as correcting a train–inference mismatch and helping identify tokens obscured by large-norm Gaussian noise.
Introduces DoubleCat, a two-level interpolant that recovers self-conditioning gains without an extra forward pass.
Extends DoubleCat with discrete reveals in SemiCat, reaching discrete diffusion-level TinyGSM performance and outperforming discrete diffusion on several likelihood evaluations at 1.7B parameters.
Also examines hybrid corruption processes and noise schedules, including asynchronous schedules.
papers.selection_reason: Analyzes design choices for continuous diffusion language models, directly relevant to LLM architectures.
papers.title: On the Design Space of Continuous Diffusion Language Models
papers.tldr: This work analyzes key design choices in continuous diffusion language models and introduces cheaper interpolants that improve token identifiability and achieve competitive performance with discrete diffusion.

papers.abstract: Clinical prognosis requires integrating structured measurements, physiological waveforms, longitudinal history, and population context. We introduce PRISM (Population-Retrieved Inference for Structured Multimodal Prognosis), a multimodal language model that combines per-feature numerical tokenization, recency-weighted aggregation of longitudinal ECGs, and a dual-modality population memory bank. Retrieval operates in representation space: the model receives mean-pooled embeddings of similar training-cohort encounters, while no individual retrieved record enters the prompt. On the 1,443-task MDS-ED benchmark, PRISM achieves AUROCs of 86.2% for diagnosis, 93.1% for deterioration, 91.8% for ICU admission, and 92.8% for mortality. These results use a 96-hour pre-arrival window unavailable to reported baselines. With benchmark-window inputs only, PRISM reaches 0.8895 AUROC, compared with 0.8937 for UniPACT and 0.8889 for MDS-ED. A matched-input compact fusion model using the same five evidence streams and frozen encoders reaches 0.7652 AUROC, versus 0.9092 for PRISM. Replacing numerical EHR encoding with text serialization reduces AUROC by 3.66 points; removing pre-arrival history reduces it by 1.97 points; and zeroing retrieval reduces it by 0.99 points. Genuine retrieval outperforms random-neighbor retrieval by 0.97 macro-average points, although a paired task-level sign test does not establish a uniform advantage (p=0.067). On the external MC-MED cohort, supervised fine-tuning reaches 0.8611 AUROC, compared with 0.8227 for locally trained gradient boosting and 0.7841 for source-only PRISM. These results support structure-aware multimodal integration and supervised external adaptation.
bullets: Addresses clinical prognosis across diagnosis, deterioration, ICU admission, and mortality using heterogeneous evidence.
Uses per-feature numerical tokenization, recency-weighted ECG history, and representation-space retrieval from a population memory bank without prompting individual records.
On MDS-ED, reports AUROCs of 86.2%–93.1% using a 96-hour pre-arrival window; with benchmark-window inputs, performance is comparable to reported baselines.

Ablations show declines from text-based numerical encoding, removing pre-arrival history, and removing retrieval; genuine retrieval improves average performance, though uniform superiority is not statistically established.
On external MC-MED data, supervised fine-tuning outperforms locally trained gradient boosting and source-only PRISM.
papers.selection_reason: The paper introduces PRISM, a multimodal language model for clinical prognosis that integrates heterogeneous evidence (waveforms, structured measurements) via a population memory bank and retrieval-augmented generation. This aligns with the 'Multimodal Foundation Models' topic, specifically the 'Multimodal Large Language Models' subtopic, as it extends LLMs to handle non-text modalities and retrieval-based context.
papers.title: Retrieval-Augmented Multimodal Language Model with Heterogeneous Evidence Integration for Clinical Prognosis
papers.tldr: PRISM integrates structured clinical data, waveforms, longitudinal history, and population retrieval to improve multimodal prognosis, with performance depending on input scope and supervised adaptation.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have taken the world by storm. Their ability to communicate with us in our own language, and to reason about our world, has made them a favorite tool for writing, answering questions, and much more. Their answers already influence our decisions and our actions. What would happen if LLMs themselves could act in the world directly? What would happen if LLMs could interact with each other? Agentic LLMs combine the power of large language models with the ability to act in the real world. In this book we will discuss how agentic LLMs work, how they act, how they interact, and what this means for us, as users.
bullets: Motivated by LLMs’ growing influence on human decisions and actions.
Explores how LLMs can act directly in the world and interact with one another.
Covers the workings, behaviors, and interactions of agentic LLMs.
Discusses implications for people who use these systems.
papers.selection_reason: Book-level treatment of agentic LLMs, relevant to large language model research and agent architectures.
papers.title: Agentic Large Language Models
papers.tldr: Agentic LLMs extend language models from generating responses to acting in and interacting with the real world.

papers.abstract: The NIST Assembly Task Board #1 remains a challenging benchmark for learning-based methods in robotic manipulation. Over short horizons, it demands precise, contact-rich control of small, tight-fitting parts. Over long horizons, it requires recovery and coordination across extended action sequences. Demonstrations, task decomposition, and dense progress rewards have enabled research advances by providing guidance on how to assemble. But how much of the strategy must be specified? The progression from AlphaGo to AlphaGo Zero showed that RL at scale can discover superhuman strategies without prescribing how to win. AlphaNIST asks whether a sparse binary task reward and task diversity admitted by this task-agnostic reward can similarly let a robot discover how to assemble. In simulation, we train a single policy from scratch across all 20 assembly tasks on the NIST Assembly Task Board #1, reaching 98.2% overall training success without demonstrations, progress shaping, scripted primitives, or per-task tuning. The framework also trains policies to complete ten assembly pairs in a single episode without a prescribed order, with task success rewarded only when all ten pairs are simultaneously complete. The learned policies discover dexterous and planning-like behaviors: choosing grasps for later assembly, using surrounding geometry to reorient parts, and preparing one part, assembling another, then returning to finish the first without an explicit planner. For videos, see our website: https://alpha-nist.github.io/
bullets: Trains from scratch on all 20 NIST Assembly Task Board #1 tasks using only binary task rewards.
Reaches 98.2% overall training success without demonstrations, progress shaping, scripted primitives, or per-task tuning.
Handles episodes containing ten assembly pairs without a prescribed order, rewarding success only when all are complete.
Discovers dexterous and planning-like behaviors, including strategic grasping, geometry-based reorientation, and task interleaving.
papers.selection_reason: Presents RL-based robotic assembly from sparse binary rewards, directly fitting robot learning and manipulation.
papers.title: AlphaNIST: Emergent Assembly Skills from Binary Task Rewards
papers.tldr: AlphaNIST shows that sparse binary rewards can drive a single robot policy to discover complex assembly strategies across diverse NIST tasks in simulation.

papers.abstract: Designing tool-integrated reasoning agent systems for complex chemical tasks remains a fundamental challenge. Although recent chemical agents have demonstrated promising performance through the integration of external tools, they are still built on the autoregressive paradigm, which is inherently constrained by causal attention and left-to-right generation. As a result, they often struggle with bidirectional molecular understanding, global coordinated tool planning and multi-source evidence integration. To address this challenge, we introduce ChemDiffAgent, the first masked diffusion language agent for tool-integrated chemical reasoning. It reformulates chemical reasoning as iterative denoising over interleaved reasoning and tool-use trajectories, enabling tool-use decisions to be jointly determined under full-trajectory context and thereby better aligning the agent's decision boundary with its knowledge boundary. We further analyze how this paradigm benefits agentic reasoning through harder infilling subproblems during training and flexible arbitrary-order decoding during inference. Then we develop a two-stage post-training framework, comprising agentic supervised fine-tuning and variance-reduced preference optimization, to enhance tool-use and reasoning capabilities. We also construct a comprehensive benchmark covering six chemistry tasks across both single-turn and multi-turn tool-use scenarios. Under matched budgets and evaluation, ChemDiffAgent consistently outperforms autoregressive agents, achieving an overall improvement of approximately 20%. Notably, our 8B model achieves performance comparable to, in some cases surpassing, significantly larger frontier models, such as GPT 5.5 and Claude Opus 4.7. Code is available at https://github.com/bilemond/ChemDiffAgent.
bullets: Targets limitations of left-to-right agents in bidirectional molecular understanding, global tool planning, and multi-source evidence integration.
Reformulates chemical reasoning as iterative denoising over interleaved reasoning and tool-use trajectories, with arbitrary-order decoding at inference.
Uses two-stage post-training: agentic supervised fine-tuning followed by variance-reduced preference optimization.
Evaluated on six chemistry tasks spanning single-turn and multi-turn tool use, with approximately 20% overall improvement under matched budgets.
The abstract reports that the 8B model performs comparably to or sometimes better than substantially larger frontier models.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a masked diffusion language agent for tool-integrated reasoning, relevant to LLM architecture and reasoning research.
papers.title: Masked Diffusion Language Agents for Tool-Integrated Chemical Reasoning
papers.tldr: ChemDiffAgent uses masked diffusion to jointly plan reasoning and tool use with full-trajectory context, improving chemical agent performance over autoregressive approaches.

papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are highly vulnerable to memory-poisoning attacks. Existing defenses primarily rely on external modules for either static memory isolation or continuous online auditing, resulting in low memory efficiency and high computational overhead. To address these limitations, inspired by neuroscientific mechanisms that weak reactivation can destabilize memories and induce decay in the absence of reinforcement, we propose an agent-intrinsic training-free memory repair framework, DREAM (Dynamic Reactivation for Engram Attenuation in Memory), that enables selective functional forgetting of poisoned memories. Specifically, DREAM implements a three-stage pipeline: perturbation-induced implicit reactivation to reveal the structural fragility of malicious memories, adaptive anomaly diagnosis based on multi-dimensional activation patterns to detect topological anomalies, and a dynamic memory repair module that selectively suppresses harmful memories while reinforcing benign ones. Extensive experiments across diverse attackers and real-world tasks demonstrate that DREAM reduces attack success rates by over 95\% against backdoor poisoning while preserving strong benign utility. DREAM also achieves competitive robustness against injection attacks. In terms of runtime and token consumption, DREAM achieves up to a 2.13$\times$ speedup and a 37.7\% reduction in token consumption compared with A-MemGuard. Furthermore, DREAM also achieves a task success rate of 92.96\% on poisoned multi-agent systems.
bullets: Addresses memory-poisoning attacks without external auditing or isolation modules.
Uses perturbation-induced reactivation, activation-pattern anomaly diagnosis, and dynamic memory repair.
Suppresses detected malicious memories while reinforcing benign memories through a training-free, agent-intrinsic process.
Reports over 95% reduction in backdoor attack success, competitive injection-attack robustness, and 92.96% task success in poisoned multi-agent systems.
Compared with A-MemGuard, achieves up to 2.13× speedup and 37.7% lower token consumption.
papers.selection_reason: Presents a training-free memory repair mechanism for selectively forgetting poisoned memories in LLM agents.
papers.title: Forgetting is Not Always Bad: A Neuro-Inspired Memory Repair Mechanism for Poisoned LLM Agents
papers.tldr: DREAM repairs poisoned LLM-agent memories by selectively forgetting harmful memories while preserving benign ones, reducing attack success and overhead.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon autonomous research has shown promise in accelerating scientific progress through sustained cycles of hypothesis generation, implementation, and validation. However, this Generate-Execute-Feedback paradigm relies on reactive trial-and-error, where costly and time-consuming executions introduce severe feedback delays, throttling evolutionary progress under explosively expanding search space. To address this challenge, we propose JANUS, a framework that unifies future outcomes forecasting and past experience reflection through a Predict-Verify-Evolve loop driven by a co-evolving world model. Within an evolving graph, the research agent proposes candidates while world model scores them by forecasting value improvement, information gain, and exploration utility, then accordingly selects, refines, or prunes branches prior to execution. After receiving ground-truth feedback, JANUS distills experience into evolving skills: hierarchical skills for research agent, exploration-strategy skills for world model, and their coordination protocols. This mechanism enables continual co-evolution: the research agent sharpens candidate generation while the world model refines its predictive judgment over extended horizons. Extensive evaluations on MLS-Bench-Lite and real research tasks demonstrate that JANUS significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, achieving both higher evolving efficiency and ceiling.
bullets: Targets feedback delays and inefficient trial-and-error in Generate–Execute–Feedback research loops.
Uses a Predict–Verify–Evolve loop within an evolving graph to forecast value improvement, information gain, and exploration utility.
Selects, refines, or prunes candidate branches before execution, then incorporates ground-truth feedback.
Co-evolves hierarchical research skills, exploration strategies, and coordination protocols for the agent and world model.
Evaluations on MLS-Bench-Lite and real research tasks report higher evolving efficiency and ceiling than state-of-the-art baselines.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes co-evolving world models that forecast action-conditioned outcomes for long-horizon research agents.
papers.title: JANUS: Enhancing Long-Horizon Autonomous Research with Co-Evolving World Models
papers.tldr: JANUS accelerates long-horizon autonomous research by using a co-evolving world model to predict, filter, and improve research candidates before costly execution.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in multimodal foundation models have made them capable generalist physical agents for a range of manipulation tasks. However, successful operation in an unfamiliar environment may require an agent to seek task-relevant information through interaction when it is absent from the observations: it may need to determine where a relevant object is, inspect an unobserved property, or discover the effect of an unfamiliar tool. We thus introduce RoboQuest, a benchmark for goal-directed embodied exploration, where agents must actively acquire task-relevant information through physical interaction, use the resulting evidence to adapt subsequent actions, and autonomously decide when to commit to task completion. RoboQuest comprises ten mobile manipulation tasks centered on three forms of uncertainty: search, manipulation-based inspection, and interactive testing. We evaluate five frontier multimodal agents through a common visuomotor interface, as well as a $π_{0.5}$ policy fine-tuned on the full-episode demonstrations we release. The best agent succeeds in only 23\% of the episodes, and the fine-tuned policy almost never succeeds. Isolated tests of the execution skills the tasks are built from, with the hidden information supplied, show that the agents can carry out most of the required actions, and our failure analysis attributes only a minority of the failures to execution. Our failure analysis further finds that the agents often stop exploring too early as they make decisions before observing the required evidence for task completion. We also find that agents rarely prevent or repair the disturbances caused by their exploration. Moreover, learning by trial and error remains difficult for most models.
bullets: Introduces ten mobile-manipulation tasks spanning search, manipulation-based inspection, and interactive testing.
Agents must acquire task-relevant evidence, adapt actions, and decide when to complete a task.
Evaluates five multimodal agents and a fine-tuned π₀.₅ policy through a common visuomotor interface.
The best agent succeeds in only 23% of episodes, while the fine-tuned policy almost never succeeds.
Failures primarily involve stopping exploration too early, neglecting disturbances, and difficulty learning through trial and error.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark for embodied exploration and mobile manipulation with multimodal agents and fine-tuned VLA policies.
papers.title: RoboQuest: Generalist Physical Agents that Search, Inspect and Test
papers.tldr: RoboQuest benchmarks whether embodied agents can actively search, inspect, and test in unfamiliar environments, revealing major gaps in information-seeking and adaptive exploration.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have become a central paradigm for robot policy learning, which predict actions in three forms: raw action chunks, discrete action tokens, or continuous action latents. However, existing action representations primarily model action trajectories, with limited consideration of the visual dynamics induced by these actions. We introduce ViDAL, a Visual Dynamics-grounded Action Latent Space that anchors continuous action latents in the future visual dynamics of the scene. Specifically, ViDAL learns action latent space by training an Action Variational Autoencoder (Action VAE) to reconstruct action chunks while aligning its latent with future scene dynamics. When integrated into downstream robot policies, the proposed Action VAE serves as a plug-in action interface compatible with multiple VLA architectures and enables optional future-video prediction as an additional capability. Empirically, ViDAL outperforms competitive baselines on LIBERO with 98.1% average success, improves a multi-task $π_{0.5}$ policy on RoboTwin 2.0 from 54.3% to 65.5% (Clean) and from 33.2% to 43.1% (Random) success rates over 50 dual-arm tasks, and yields 20.0% and 23.4% absolute success-rate gains on real-world single-arm Franka and dual-arm ARX robot platforms.
bullets: Existing VLA action representations mainly model trajectories without explicitly capturing the visual dynamics actions induce.
ViDAL trains an Action VAE to reconstruct action chunks while aligning its latent space with future scene dynamics.
The resulting plug-in action interface is compatible with multiple VLA architectures and can optionally support future-video prediction.
ViDAL achieves 98.1% average success on LIBERO and improves π₀.₅ on RoboTwin 2.0 from 54.3% to 65.5% (Clean) and 33.2% to 43.1% (Random).
It also reports absolute success-rate gains on real-world Franka and ARX robot platforms, though the abstract does not specify the baseline setup or broader limitations.
papers.selection_reason: Directly addresses VLA models and robot policy learning with an action latent space grounded in visual dynamics.
papers.title: ViDAL: A Visual Dynamics-Grounded Action Latent Space for Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.tldr: ViDAL learns action latents grounded in predicted future visual dynamics, improving vision-language-action robot policies across simulated and real-world tasks.

papers.abstract: Full-duplex voice agents make many small, closed decisions, which current systems answer by slow autoregressive decoding. We propose DuplexJev, which feeds ASR-encoder hidden states through a small connector into a frozen LLM and reads each question as a single-token distribution over its options. Nothing is decoded, and an 8-GPU node answers 80 decisions about eight utterances in about 0.1 s. With a last-layer connector, spoken QA stays close to reading the transcript (90% vs. 91%). DuplexJev also hears the speaker: gender and emotion accuracy both reach 90% (from 55% and 28%) with a cross-attention connector, whose spoken QA drops by only 1 point (83% to 82%). We train decisions with cross-entropy on the read-out answer token, instead of the usual transcript distillation, whose teacher never hears the voice, and keep distillation for content. Encoders and LLMs are interchangeable; we release weights, training recipe, a batched-inference pipeline for full-duplex serving and a bilingual spoken-QA set.
bullets: Maps ASR-encoder representations into a frozen LLM and reads each question as a single-token option distribution.
Uses answer-token cross-entropy for decision supervision while retaining distillation for speech content.
Handles spoken QA, speaker gender, and emotion, with cross-attention improving paralinguistic recognition while slightly reducing QA accuracy.
Batches 80 decisions over eight utterances in about 0.1 seconds on an 8-GPU node.
Provides interchangeable encoder/LLM components, released weights and recipe, a full-duplex inference pipeline, and a bilingual spoken-QA set.
papers.selection_reason: Extends a frozen LLM with speech encoder features for batched single-token decisions; fits multimodal LLMs and efficient inference.
papers.title: Batched Speech Decisions Without Decoding: Single-Token Supervision Lets a Frozen LLM Hear Beyond the Transcript
papers.tldr: DuplexJev enables a frozen LLM to answer many speech-based decisions in parallel from ASR hidden states without autoregressive decoding.

papers.abstract: Muon improves large-scale training by applying a spectral-norm steepest-descent update to matrix parameters, but practical models also contain parameter blocks that do not fit dense-matrix geometry. One important case is the tied vocabulary table, which appears in language models and other token generators and can receive multiple structurally different gradient sources, from sparse input lookups to dense output-classifier updates. In the reference recipe these blocks are handed to an auxiliary AdamW optimizer, which restores second-moment state and updates the aliased table as a generic tensor. We propose AF-Muon, an AdamW-free extension of Muon that keeps the Muon matrix update for hidden weight matrices while using a support-aware finite-cap linear minimization oracle for tied vocabulary tables and an RMS-normalized update for one-dimensional auxiliary parameters. AF-Muon therefore trains every parameter class with a single first-moment buffer and no second-moment state, saving around 20% optimizer-state memory relative to Hybrid Muon in our benchmark. Across nine tied-token settings - decoder-only language models from 124M to 1B parameters, a fully shared T5-style encoder-decoder, and ImageGPT-style image-token, protein, and sparse-MoE variants, spanning text, image, and protein-sequence data - AF-Muon improves mean validation loss and perplexity over both Hybrid Muon and a SCION-style Sign endpoint. Long-horizon runs and hyperparameter sensitivity studies confirm the gain is robust, and identical-momentum diagnostics attribute it to the finite cap, which preserves more within-row magnitude than Sign while bounding the coordinate concentration of row-RMS. These results identify tied vocabulary tables as a distinct optimizer geometry and yield a robust AdamW-free Muon variant across models, modalities, and architectures, with about 1% step-time overhead in matched training.
bullets: Addresses tied vocabulary tables that receive both sparse input-lookup and dense output-classifier gradients.
Keeps Muon updates for matrix weights, uses a support-aware finite-cap oracle for tied tables, and RMS-normalized updates for 1D parameters.
Uses only first-moment state, saving around 20% optimizer-state memory versus Hybrid Muon.
Improves mean validation loss and perplexity across nine tied-token settings, including language, image, protein, encoder-decoder, and sparse-MoE models.
Reported overhead is about 1% of matched training step time; diagnostics attribute gains to the finite cap preserving within-row magnitude while limiting coordinate concentration.
papers.selection_reason: Presents an optimizer that reduces memory and compute overhead for tied-embedding models; fits efficient AI via reduced training memory and step-time cost.
papers.title: AF-Muon: An AdamW-Free Muon Optimizer for Tied-Embedding Models
papers.tldr: AF-Muon extends Muon to tied-embedding models without AdamW, reducing optimizer-state memory while improving validation performance across diverse modalities and architectures.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have achieved high task success rates on robot manipulation task benchmarks. More recently, there has been an emphasis on evaluating the robustness of VLA models to perturbations. However, this robustness is still predominantly measured through Task Success Rate (TSR). In this work, we propose a benchmark-agnostic evaluation framework to measure the behavioural robustness of models by characterising how successful trajectories are executed under perturbation. We implement this methodology by extending the widely-used LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus benchmarks. Across three state-of-the-art VLA models, four LIBERO task suites and seven perturbation conditions, we evaluate changes in both typical successful behaviour and its variability, including metrics of motion smoothness, efficiency and gripper behaviour. We find that perturbations can alter the behaviour of successful trajectories, a phenomenon which cannot necessarily be inferred from TSR alone. Across LIBERO suites, we identify cases where state-of-the-art VLA models achieve comparable TSR under the same perturbation condition, yet behaviour on successful trajectories diverges substantially. Therefore, to have a more robust assessment of task performance, we argue that suitable measures of robustness should capture not only whether a task is completed, but also how the robot behaves while completing it. When evaluating the robustness of VLA models, TSR may be complemented by behavioural evaluation metrics that characterise the nature and variability of successful task execution by robots.
bullets: Introduces a benchmark-agnostic framework for evaluating behavioural robustness in tabletop manipulation.
Extends LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus across four task suites, seven perturbation conditions, and three VLA models.
Analyses motion smoothness, efficiency, gripper behaviour, and variability in successful trajectories.
Finds that perturbations can substantially change successful behaviour even when task success rates remain comparable.
Argues that behavioural metrics should complement task success rate for more complete robustness assessment.
papers.selection_reason: Evaluates behavioral robustness of VLA models under perturbations in tabletop manipulation; directly fits VLA and robot learning.
papers.title: Is Success All You Need? Investigating the Impact of Input Perturbations on VLA Behaviour in Tabletop Manipulation Tasks
papers.tldr: VLA robustness evaluation should measure how robots complete successful tasks under perturbations, not just whether they succeed.

papers.abstract: Prior-free 6D object pose tracking seeks to recover the trajectory of an unseen object from a single RGB video without object-specific CAD models, posed reference images, or pose annotations. Geometric foundation models provide complementary object-centric and scene-centric cues, yet SAM3D CAD is indexed by an arbitrary object-local surface parameterization, whereas reconstructed evidence is expressed in a sequence-specific world frame with partial surface coverage. To exploit this complementarity, we formulate tracking as generation-reconstruction correspondence and introduce GRC-Pose, a correspondence-based framework that combines learned correspondence prediction with robust pose estimation. Concretely, GeoCorr-Matcher estimates weighted object-scene correspondences and per-match uncertainty for each pose candidate. FGH-Solver integrates these matches through multiple robust geometric estimators and sequence-level posterior inference, while a posterior-gated memory retains only inlier-supported observations through occlusion and viewpoint change. Extensive evaluation shows that with SAM3D CAD, GRC-Pose achieves state-of-the-art Average Recall and motion retention on HOT3D, improving the latter by 58% over prior art. On classical benchmarks including YCBInEOAT and LINEMOD, it remains highly competitive.
bullets: Addresses prior-free 6D pose tracking without CAD models, posed references, or pose annotations.
Predicts weighted object–scene correspondences and per-match uncertainty for candidate poses.
Combines robust geometric estimators with sequence-level posterior inference for pose estimation.
Uses posterior-gated memory to retain inlier-supported observations during occlusion and viewpoint changes.
Achieves state-of-the-art Average Recall and motion retention on HOT3D, with 58% higher motion retention than prior work; remains competitive on YCBInEOAT and LINEMOD.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes prior-free 6D object pose tracking using geometric foundation models and correspondence; directly fits 3D perception and geometry.
papers.title: GRC-Pose: Generation-Reconstruction Correspondence for Prior-Free 6D Object Pose Tracking
papers.tldr: GRC-Pose tracks unseen objects in 6D from a single RGB video without object-specific pose priors by matching generated object geometry to reconstructed scene evidence.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have advanced robotic manipulation, but their zero-shot generalization in new tasks and environments remains limited, and their reliance on specialized training keeps them from benefiting directly from rapidly advancing general-purpose vision-language models (VLMs). In parallel, recent agentic robotic systems leverage VLMs for high-level reasoning or coding agents for robot control, but often depend on extensive external models and tools, introducing additional complexity and cost. This motivates us to ask: Can a general-purpose VLM itself operate a robot more like the human teleoperator by reasoning directly from observations, issuing actions, and continuously adapting to execution feedback, without relying on external models such as learned action experts, coding agents or grounding tools like SAM3? In this work, we introduce MotorMind, a robot manipulation harness that connects VLM-proposed mid-level actions to deterministic robot control and feedback, with asynchronous monitoring and background memory updates. Without task-specific policy training, coding agents, or additional grounding tools such as SAM3, MotorMind achieves 66.7% success on the base LIBERO-PRO suites and 53.8% under perturbations, compared with at most 13.3% and 19.2%, respectively, for the prior zero-shot methods we evaluate. The same interface reaches 95% average success on a real xArm6 robot across direct manipulation and human-perturbation settings. Replacing the backbone with a stronger VLM further improves performance, while the remaining failures - primarily due to visual grounding, embodied reasoning, and action knowledge - decrease as VLM capability improves. These results show that a general-purpose VLM, when equipped with an appropriate mid-level action representation and asynchronous execution harness, can perform effective zero-shot robotic manipulation.
bullets: Targets limited zero-shot generalization and the complexity of systems requiring specialized policies, coding agents, or grounding tools.
Uses a robot manipulation harness with VLM-proposed mid-level actions, deterministic control, asynchronous monitoring, and background memory updates.
Achieves 66.7% success on base LIBERO-PRO and 53.8% under perturbations, versus at most 13.3% and 19.2% for evaluated prior zero-shot methods.
Reaches 95% average success on a real xArm6 across direct manipulation and human-perturbation settings.
Performance improves with stronger VLMs; remaining failures mainly involve visual grounding, embodied reasoning, and action knowledge.
papers.selection_reason: Directly addresses zero-shot robot manipulation by connecting general VLMs to mid-level actions and feedback, fitting VLA and robot learning/manipulation.
papers.title: MotorMind: Scaffolding General Vision Language Models for Zero-Shot Robot Manipulation
papers.tldr: MotorMind enables a general-purpose VLM to perform zero-shot robot manipulation by converting mid-level action reasoning into controlled execution with feedback and memory.

papers.abstract: Agent skills provide a lightweight mechanism for self-evolving agents to accumulate reusable procedural knowledge without updating model parameters. However, existing learned skill curators typically optimize curation without explicitly modeling downstream executor behavior. We show that this can cause systematic cross-executor degradation: curators trained with different executors perform best when paired with their own training executor, indicating that effective skill curation is executor-dependent. We formulate behavior-adaptive skill curation and introduce EASE, a framework that learns a single curator that adapts its decisions to different executor behaviors. EASE maintains an online behavioral profile of recent execution patterns and conditions the curator on this profile, the current trajectory, and retrieved skills to add, modify, or remove skills from an evolving repository. We train the shared curator jointly across multiple frozen executors with reinforcement learning, using retrieval-aware and behavior-aware temporal attribution to focus optimization on curation actions with observable downstream influence. Across ALFWorld, ScienceWorld, and WebShop, with executors ranging from Qwen3-8B/32B and GPT-OSS-120B to unseen Kimi K2.6, DeepSeek V4 Flash, and Gemini 3.5 Flash, EASE outperforms strong skill- and memory-based baselines without per-executor finetuning. EASE also maintains 34.5--41.0% fewer skills, improves skill retrieval by 36.3--38.7% and measured edit utility by 51.8--60.0%, and reduces deployment-time inference tokens by 9.1--14.5%. These results establish behavior-adaptive skill curation as an effective principle for building self-evolving agents.
bullets: Existing curators can degrade performance when paired with executors different from those used in training.
EASE maintains an online profile of executor behavior and conditions curation on that profile, the current trajectory, and retrieved skills.
A shared curator is jointly trained across frozen executors using retrieval- and behavior-aware reinforcement-learning attribution.
Across ALFWorld, ScienceWorld, and WebShop, EASE outperforms skill- and memory-based baselines, including on unseen executors.
EASE uses 34.5–41.0% fewer skills, improves retrieval by 36.3–38.7% and edit utility by 51.8–60.0%, and reduces inference tokens by 9.1–14.5%.
papers.selection_reason: Behavior-adaptive skill curation enables self-evolving agents to continuously adapt; matches online/continual learning focus.
papers.title: EASE: Behavior-Adaptive Skill Curation for Self-Evolving Agents
papers.tldr: EASE enables one skill curator to adapt to different agent executors, improving skill quality and efficiency without per-executor fine-tuning.

papers.abstract: Ultrasound (US) acquisition depends on the operator's ability to interpret anatomy and anticipate how the view will change with probe motion. Many robotic US navigation methods select actions without explicitly predicting these anatomical changes. We propose SonoGraph-WM, an action- and goal-conditioned world model for anticipatory probe navigation. The model represents anatomy as scene graphs (SGs), capturing visible structures, their geometry, and spatial relationships without synthesizing US images. Given a history of SGs and probe poses, a unified Transformer jointly predicts future SGs and poses. A receding-horizon planner recursively imagines candidate trajectories, selects the shortest predicted path reaching a goal graph, and follows it over a short execution horizon before replanning from new observations. To reduce reliance on tracked and anatomically annotated US sequences, we generate aligned SG--pose training data from computed tomography (CT) label maps along surface-constrained probe trajectories. On four held-out CT cases, spatial relation F1 remains above 93% over 20 prediction steps, and closed-loop navigation achieves 77.50% and 75.00% success for the gallbladder and pancreas, respectively, using annotation-derived SGs. In robot--phantom navigation experiments with label-map-derived SGs, the planner reached the target view in 73.7% of trials. These findings support CT-supervised anatomical world modeling for probe planning and highlight the importance of frequent observation updates for reliable navigation. Project Page: https://noseefood.github.io/us-sonograph-wm/
bullets: Represents ultrasound anatomy as scene graphs of visible structures, geometry, and spatial relationships instead of synthesizing images.
A unified Transformer predicts future scene graphs and probe poses from observation histories; receding-horizon planning selects and repeatedly updates trajectories toward a goal graph.
CT label maps generate aligned scene-graph/pose training data, reducing dependence on tracked and anatomically annotated ultrasound sequences.
On held-out CT cases, spatial-relation F1 stayed above 93% for 20 prediction steps; navigation success was 77.50% for the gallbladder and 75.00% for the pancreas.
Robot–phantom trials reached target views in 73.7% of cases, with results emphasizing frequent observation updates for reliable navigation.
papers.selection_reason: Action-conditioned scene-graph world model for anticipatory robotic ultrasound navigation; aligns with interactive world models and robot navigation.
papers.title: Scanning While Imagining: A Scene-Graph World Model for Robotic Ultrasound Navigation
papers.tldr: SonoGraph-WM enables anticipatory robotic ultrasound navigation by predicting future anatomical scene graphs and probe poses, then planning through imagined trajectories.

papers.abstract: Hybrid language models maintain fixed-size recurrent states, but existing quantizers typically use eight bits or more. Quantization errors persist according to channel decay rates. We derive distortion weights from the observability Gramian and combine them with normalized state ranges for mixed-precision bit allocation, without calibration data, rotation, or training. We also quantize decay rates logarithmically. With per-token state quantization, a four-bit mean payload reduces excess negative log-likelihood by factors of 3.3--27.9 relative to the best of seven baselines across three hybrid models; metadata costs vary. At six bits, negative log-likelihood differs from the FP32-state baseline by less than 0.005 nats. Ablations separate gains from variable bit widths, decay weighting, and range normalization. With less frequent write-backs, gains diminish and depend on the model and budget.
bullets: Existing recurrent-state quantizers generally use at least eight bits, while persistent errors depend on channel decay rates.
The method allocates bits using observability-Gramian distortion weights and normalized state ranges, and logarithmically quantizes decay rates.
It requires no calibration data, rotations, or retraining, and supports per-token state quantization.
Across three hybrid models, four-bit mean payloads reduce excess negative log-likelihood by 3.3–27.9× versus seven baselines; metadata costs vary.
At six bits, negative log-likelihood is within 0.005 nats of the FP32-state baseline; benefits diminish with less frequent write-backs and depend on model and budget.
papers.selection_reason: Low-bit quantization of recurrent states in hybrid language models reduces memory footprint; directly relevant to memory-efficient inference.
papers.title: Low-Bit Recurrent States in Hybrid Language Models
papers.tldr: A calibration-free mixed-precision quantizer enables accurate low-bit recurrent states in hybrid language models, with four-bit states substantially reducing quantization error and six-bit states nearly matching FP32 performance.

papers.abstract: Aerial manipulation in outdoor environments remains challenging due to the simultaneous requirements of reliable state estimation, stable aerial motion, and precise manipulation under external disturbances. In this work, we present a real-world outdoor aerial manipulation framework that integrates imitation learning, onboard LiDAR-inertial state estimation, and whole-body model predictive control. A Diffusion Policy is trained from manipulation demonstrations to generate desired end-effector motions from onboard observations. These learned commands are executed by a whole-body MPC that jointly coordinates the aerial platform and manipulator to realize the desired end-effector trajectory. To eliminate reliance on external motion-capture infrastructure, the platform employs onboard LiDAR-inertial odometry for state estimation during outdoor operation. We validate the complete framework on a physical aerial manipulator and demonstrate successful execution of outdoor manipulation tasks. The experimental results show that demonstration-driven manipulation policies can be effectively integrated with onboard state estimation and model-based whole-body control to enable aerial manipulation beyond controlled indoor environments.
bullets: Addresses outdoor aerial manipulation under disturbances, where state estimation, flight stability, and precise interaction must work together.
Uses a Diffusion Policy trained from demonstrations to generate desired end-effector motions from onboard observations.
Combines LiDAR-inertial odometry with whole-body model predictive control to coordinate the aerial vehicle and manipulator without motion capture.
Validated on a physical aerial manipulator through successful outdoor manipulation tasks.
Demonstrates feasibility beyond controlled indoor environments; the abstract does not quantify performance or specify task and environmental limits.
papers.selection_reason: Integrated imitation learning, onboard perception, and whole-body MPC for outdoor aerial manipulation; strong fit with robot learning and manipulation.
papers.title: Aerial Manipulation in the Wild with Onboard Perception, Policy Learning, and Whole-Body Control
papers.tldr: An integrated learning-and-control framework enables an aerial manipulator to perform outdoor tasks using only onboard perception and whole-body control.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) provide limited support for sign language interaction. Unifying sign language translation (SLT) and generation (SLG) to enable sign language as both input and output can reduce switching between separate models during sign-text interaction. We present SignGPT, a unified, pose-based framework for gloss-free SLT and SLG. SignGPT integrates part-aware hierarchical representations of body, hand, and facial motion into a shared language model and employs asymmetric multi-token prediction and progressive training for bidirectional modeling. We evaluate SignGPT on How2Sign (ASL) and Phoenix-2014T (DGS) through benchmark comparisons, qualitative analyses, and component ablations. An exploratory study with 12 Deaf ASL signers assesses an LLM-mediated sign-to-sign response pipeline, highlighting the potential of unified modeling to support sign language conversation (SLC).
bullets: Targets limited LLM support for sign language and the need to combine translation and generation.
Uses part-aware hierarchical representations of body, hand, and facial motion within a shared language model.
Applies asymmetric multi-token prediction and progressive training for bidirectional modeling.
Evaluated on How2Sign (ASL) and Phoenix-2014T (DGS) with benchmark comparisons, qualitative analysis, and ablations.
A 12-person Deaf ASL signer study explores its potential for sign-to-sign conversational interaction.
papers.selection_reason: Unifies sign language translation and generation through an LLM with multimodal pose understanding; fits multimodal large language models.
papers.title: SignGPT: Toward LLM-Mediated Sign Language Interaction through Gloss-Free Translation and Generation
papers.tldr: SignGPT unifies gloss-free sign language translation and generation in one pose-based, LLM-mediated framework to support bidirectional sign-text and sign-to-sign interaction.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive generation of interleaved text and acoustic tokens is a common approach to spoken-response generation in speech large language models. Although this design enables streaming generation with explicit textual guidance, generated acoustic tokens become part of the context for subsequent text predictions. Given identical speech inputs, we observe markedly lower answer accuracy for the internal text generated in speech-to-text-and-speech (S2TS) mode than for speech-to-text (S2T) responses. We term this discrepancy the \emph{output-mode gap} (OMG). To reduce OMG, we propose \emph{Joint-Output On-Policy Distillation} (JO-OPD), which distills the model's stronger S2T policy into joint generation using student-generated S2TS trajectories. At each text position, the S2T teacher provides soft targets from a text-only projection of the student's preceding outputs, while the student predicts from the corresponding full interleaved history. A preservation objective further regularizes native non-text predictions. Experiments on Step-Audio-2-mini and Baichuan-Audio-Instruct reveal OMG across two interleaved generation architectures. On Step-Audio-2-mini, JO-OPD reduces OMG from 42.87 to 16.26 percentage points on Spoken-MQA and from 29.72 to 13.04 points on speech-rendered GSM8K, with little change in S2T accuracy and substantially larger reductions than matched SFT baselines. ASR-based evaluation further shows a 7.49-point improvement in spoken-answer accuracy on Spoken-MQA.
bullets: The output-mode gap arises because generated acoustic tokens remain in the context and degrade later text predictions.
JO-OPD uses student-generated S2TS trajectories and soft targets from an S2T teacher based on text-only histories.
A preservation objective regularizes the model’s native non-text predictions during distillation.
On Step-Audio-2-mini, the gap fell from 42.87 to 16.26 points on Spoken-MQA and from 29.72 to 13.04 points on speech-rendered GSM8K.
S2T accuracy changed little, while ASR evaluation showed a 7.49-point Spoken-MQA improvement; results cover two interleaved-generation architectures.
papers.selection_reason: Speech language models with interleaved text and audio generation are multimodal LLMs, and the distillation method targets a core multimodal generation challenge.
papers.title: Reducing the Output-Mode Gap in Speech Language Models via Joint-Output On-Policy Distillation
papers.tldr: JO-OPD narrows the accuracy gap between speech-to-text-and-speech and speech-to-text generation by distilling a stronger text-only policy into interleaved speech generation.

papers.abstract: Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) reporting is critical for corporate accountability, with Large Language Models (LLMs) and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) offering strong potential to automate KPI extraction. However, open-source LLM performance in domain-specific ESG tasks remains insufficiently understood. This paper evaluates open-source LLMs in ESG contexts using a structured framework and evaluation resource based on 498 real-world ESG reports from EU-listed companies (2010-2024). We evaluate seven open-source models (2B to 30B parameters) -- glm-4.7-flash, nemotron-3-nano:4b, qwen3:4b-instruct, gemma3:4b, gemma4:e4b, gemma4:e2b, and ministral-3:8b -- using 100 persona-based synthetic QA pairs covering ESG information needs. System performance is assessed via RAGAS metrics, including contextual recall, precision, relevance, faithfulness, answer relevancy, and factual correctness. Results show notable performance variations across architectures. Retrieval performance is strong across models (context recall around 0.58-0.61, context precision around 0.78-0.81, context relevance 0.965-0.985). Generation diverges most on faithfulness (0.607-0.822) and least on answer relevancy (0.760-0.881): glm-4.7-flash leads in faithfulness (0.822), qwen3 in factual correctness (0.449), and ministral-3 in answer relevancy (0.881). Low overall factual correctness (0.387-0.449) highlights the need for domain-specific fine-tuning. This work provides data-driven guidance for deploying open-source models in ESG reporting.
bullets: Evaluates open-source LLMs for ESG KPI extraction using 498 EU-listed-company reports from 2010–2024 and 100 persona-based QA pairs.
Assesses RAG with RAGAS metrics covering retrieval quality, faithfulness, answer relevancy, and factual correctness.
Retrieval performance is consistently strong across models, while generation varies substantially by architecture.
glm-4.7-flash leads in faithfulness, qwen3 in factual correctness, and ministral-3 in answer relevancy.
Low factual-correctness scores indicate that domain-specific fine-tuning is still needed for dependable ESG reporting automation.
papers.selection_reason: Empirical evaluation of retrieval-augmented generation directly concerns external-memory retrieval and generation behavior in language models.
papers.title: Empirical Evaluation of Open-Source Large Language Models for Retrieval-Augmented Generation in ESG Domain
papers.tldr: A systematic evaluation of seven open-source LLMs finds that RAG retrieves ESG information reliably, but generation quality—especially factual correctness—remains limited and model-dependent.

papers.abstract: We propose a linearized Physics-Informed Neural Network (lPINN), a reduced-order neural basis method for forward and inverse differential equations. In an offline stage, lPINN learns operator-compatible continuous neural basis functions from an ensemble of numerical solutions. The basis functions are differentiable through automatic differentiation and are pretrained using solution data together with either derivative information or physics residuals. For each new problem instance, the basis functions are frozen and the solution is obtained by minimizing the governing-equation residual together with applicable initial, boundary, regularization, and observational terms. Unlike surrogate and operator-learning methods, the training data define the trial space offline, while the instance-specific solution is computed online by enforcing the governing physics. Relative to vanilla PINNs, lPINN pretrains the nonlinear hidden-layer representation offline and performs online inference only in the final linear layer. We evaluate lPINN on forward and inverse problems for the advection-diffusion equation, Burgers' equation, and the nonlinear pendulum equation. Compared with vanilla PINNs, lPINN achieves lower solution and parameter errors while reducing online inference times by approximately one to more than three orders of magnitude, with the largest gains generally observed for limited residual or measurement data. Cross-resolution experiments show that the learned continuous representation can be evaluated on finer meshes without retraining and with nearly unchanged accuracy.
bullets: Targets faster and more data-efficient solution of forward and inverse differential equations than vanilla PINNs.
Learns differentiable, operator-compatible basis functions from ensembles of numerical solutions, derivative data, or physics residuals.
Freezes the nonlinear representation for each new instance; online optimization enforces governing equations and relevant initial, boundary, observational, and regularization terms.
Evaluated on advection-diffusion, Burgers’, and nonlinear pendulum equations.

Compared with vanilla PINNs, reports lower solution and parameter errors and online speedups of roughly one to over three orders of magnitude, especially with limited residual or measurement data; supports finer meshes without retraining.
papers.selection_reason: Instance-specific online residual minimization over frozen pretrained layers is a test-time optimization method with substantial inference-speed gains.
papers.title: Linearized PINN with pretrained nonlinear layers
papers.tldr: lPINN pretrains physics-compatible neural basis functions offline, then solves new forward or inverse differential-equation problems online using only a linear output layer and physics constraints.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in data-driven robot manipulation policies have substantially improved task execution and generalization. However, real-world deployment still relies heavily on humans for failure assessment, correction, and environment reset, while models often fail to continually learn from failures and corrective experience. We present REVOLVE (Robot Evolving via Orchestrated Loops, Verification, and Experience), an automated closed-loop framework for evolving robot manipulation with minimal human intervention. Built on a unified software platform, REVOLVE integrates data collection, policy training and deployment, failure recovery, and continual learning into a single closed-loop workflow. Its Automated Reset and Correction (ARC) architecture automatically resets the environment and intervenes to correct policy failures. Dual-Loop Evolution (DLE) continually improves the manipulation policy and agent by feeding real-world interaction and failure--correction data back into policy learning and using an external mismatch memory to refine agent judgments. Experiments across four real-world manipulation tasks show that, after five iterations, REVOLVE improves average policy success rate by 18.5% and agent judgment accuracy by 8.5%, while reducing human effort in data collection and deployment testing by 94.4% and 95.1%, respectively. These results demonstrate that REVOLVE transforms real-world deployment into a closed-loop learning process that continually accumulates and uses execution experience, enabling continual evolution of both the policy and supervisory model with substantially less human intervention.
bullets: Addresses the need for humans to assess failures, correct behavior, and reset environments during real-world deployment.
Integrates data collection, policy training/deployment, failure recovery, and continual learning in one workflow.
Uses Automated Reset and Correction (ARC) for recovery and Dual-Loop Evolution (DLE) to improve both manipulation policies and agent judgments.
Across four real-world tasks and five iterations, average policy success rose 18.5% and judgment accuracy rose 8.5%.
Human effort in data collection and deployment testing fell by 94.4% and 95.1%, respectively.
papers.selection_reason: Closed-loop continual learning framework for evolving robot manipulation with minimal human intervention.
papers.title: REVOLVE: An Automated Closed-Loop Framework for Evolving Robot Manipulation with Minimal Human Intervention
papers.tldr: REVOLVE creates a closed-loop robot manipulation system that learns from failures and corrections while sharply reducing human involvement.

papers.abstract: Active exploration and semantic navigation require an embodied agent to build memory from partial observations, predict how the evolution of observed spatial memory may support future motion, and convert that prediction into actionable plans. We present GLAM, a goal-conditioned latent world model trained over global spatiotemporal memory, and GLAM NAV, the complete navigation system built around it. Given historical map tokens, a navigation goal, and the current robot pose, GLAM jointly predicts future map representations and robot-centric waypoint latents, allowing future spatial context and navigation intent to be inferred in a shared representation space. The model follows a JEPA-like latent prediction paradigm, operates directly on map-level latent tokens rather than RGB reconstruction, and uses a pretrained waypoint encoder-decoder to supervise and decode navigation plans within GLAM NAV. Training data are collected by replaying ObjectNav expert trajectories in Habitat over HM3D v0.2 scene assets and slicing them into multi-timescale prediction samples. On a controlled HM3D-ObjectNav subset reproduction setting, GLAM NAV improves over a reproduced BSC-Nav baseline in both success rate and success weighted by path length.
bullets: Uses historical map tokens, the navigation goal, and robot pose to jointly predict future map representations and robot-centric waypoint latents.
Applies JEPA-like latent prediction directly to map-level tokens instead of reconstructing RGB observations.
GLAM NAV combines the world model with a pretrained waypoint encoder-decoder to generate actionable navigation plans.
Trained on replayed ObjectNav expert trajectories in Habitat using HM3D v0.2 scenes and multi-timescale prediction samples.
On a controlled HM3D-ObjectNav reproduction subset, it improves success rate and success weighted by path length over a reproduced BSC-Nav baseline.
papers.selection_reason: Latent world model over global spatiotemporal memory for active exploration and navigation.
papers.title: GLAM: Training a latent world model over global spatiotemporal memory for active exploration and navigation
papers.tldr: GLAM learns a goal-conditioned latent world model that predicts future spatial memory and navigation waypoints for active exploration and semantic navigation.

papers.abstract: Autonomous Surface Vehicles (ASVs) are increasingly expected to operate in ports and harbour environments, where operators may specify navigation targets through language-based descriptions rather than predefined coordinates or fixed target identifiers. However, existing ASV navigation methods mainly execute predefined geometric goals or task-specific objectives and give limited attention to language-grounded target specification. This study proposes Semantically Grounded Navigation (SGNav), a framework that enables an ASV to identify and approach a maritime target from an operator-provided description. SGNav integrates text-guided semantic grounding, harbour-aware candidate filtering, CLIP-based semantic verification, grounded target control-state construction, and Proximal Policy Optimisation-based closed-loop control. It grounds the target description in onboard RGB observations, suppresses visually or semantically irrelevant distractors, and converts the selected target into a compact control-oriented representation for policy execution. Experiments in simulated port environments show that SGNav achieves success rates of $97.0\pm1.2\%$, $92.0\pm1.5\%$, and $90.0\pm1.8\%$ across three representative target-reaching tasks, with semantic target accuracy above $97\%$ and wrong-target rates below $3\%$. SGNav also maintains $97.7$--$98.7\%$ success rates across held-out port layouts. In the Task~3 ablation study, removing harbour-aware filtering or semantic consistency reduces the success rate to $40.4\pm2.6\%$ and $50.4\pm3.1\%$, respectively. These findings demonstrate the importance of semantic grounding, harbour-aware filtering, and semantic verification for reliable language-grounded ASV navigation. These results indicate that the proposed perception-to-control framework can support language-grounded target approach manoeuvres of ASV under the complex port environments.
bullets: Addresses the gap between language-specified navigation targets and conventional coordinate- or task-based ASV navigation.
Uses text-guided grounding, harbour-aware candidate filtering, CLIP-based verification, and PPO control from RGB observations.
Achieves 90.0–97.0% success across three simulated port tasks, with over 97% semantic target accuracy and under 3% wrong-target rates.
Maintains 97.7–98.7% success on held-out port layouts.
Ablations show substantial degradation without harbour-aware filtering or semantic consistency, indicating their importance.
papers.selection_reason: Language-grounded semantic target navigation for autonomous surface vehicles.
papers.title: Language-Grounded Semantic Target Navigation for Autonomous Surface Vehicles
papers.tldr: SGNav enables autonomous surface vehicles to navigate to maritime targets described in natural language by combining semantic perception, target verification, and closed-loop control.

papers.abstract: Mobile robots typically rely on geometric maps for obstacle avoidance and path planning, but the resulting obstacle representation does not always match how an object should affect navigation. A low lying cable may be missed, a flexible curtain may create spurious blockage, and a traffic cone may require an exclusion region larger than its observed footprint. We present NavPatch, an object level correction layer that assigns ADD, REMOVE, or EXTEND to navigation relevant object categories through periodic scene understanding with a vision-language model. Open vocabulary grounding localizes object instances, and LiDAR and RGB-D observations provide 3D support. Observation quality filtering and cross frame maintenance determine when each correction patch is committed, replaced, or revoked. In 50 real robot trials across five layouts, NavPatch achieves an overall success rate of 86.0%. An ablation study of four configurations with 200 runs in total shows that NavPatch improves the success rate from 70.0% to 86.0% and reduces the false commit rate from 68.4% to 40.7% compared with updates based only on the current observation.
bullets: Addresses mismatches between geometric obstacle maps and how objects should affect navigation.
Assigns object-level ADD, REMOVE, or EXTEND corrections using open-vocabulary grounding with LiDAR and RGB-D support.
Filters observation quality and maintains corrections across frames before committing, replacing, or revoking patches.
In 50 real-robot trials across five layouts, achieved an 86.0% overall success rate.
Across 200 ablation runs, improved success from 70.0% to 86.0% and reduced false commits from 68.4% to 40.7% versus current-observation-only updates.
papers.selection_reason: VLM-grounded object-level costmap correction for mobile robot obstacle avoidance and navigation.
papers.title: NavPatch: Evidence-Guided Object-Level Costmap Correction with Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: NavPatch uses vision-language scene understanding and 3D sensing to dynamically correct object-level navigation costmaps, improving robot navigation success and reducing erroneous map updates.

papers.abstract: Video segmentation models recognize and track objects over time, but they do not indicate whether each segmented region moves independently of the observing camera. This dynamicity attribute cannot be inferred from semantics alone and is confounded by camera ego-motion. We introduce \method, an online framework that augments query-based video segmentation with region-level dynamicity prediction. It jointly produces the original segmentation outputs and a dynamic or static state for each predicted region. At inference, DynEoMT uses only the current frame and propagated queries, without optical flow, depth, camera pose, previous RGB frames, or feature maps. Because established video segmentation benchmarks do not annotate this attribute, we also introduce a class-agnostic offline supervision pipeline using camera-compensated optical flow and confidence-aware temporal filtering. Across VIPSeg, OVIS, YouTube-VIS 2022, and VSPW, DynEoMT achieves balanced accuracies of 84.3, 68.0, 68.6, and 87.6, respectively, while largely preserving segmentation performance. These results show that segmentation-region dynamicity can be learned from propagated queries, enabling its online prediction without a dedicated motion-processing pipeline at inference. The complete code will be released as open source to enable full reproduction of the method and experiments.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of distinguishing independently moving objects from camera-induced motion, which semantics alone cannot resolve.
Jointly predicts segmentation masks and region-level dynamicity without optical flow, depth, camera pose, previous RGB frames, or feature maps at inference.
Introduces an offline supervision pipeline based on camera-compensated optical flow and confidence-aware temporal filtering.
Evaluated on VIPSeg, OVIS, YouTube-VIS 2022, and VSPW, achieving balanced accuracies of 84.3, 68.0, 68.6, and 87.6 while largely preserving segmentation performance.
papers.selection_reason: Online video segmentation with region-level dynamicity prediction; temporal video understanding.
papers.title: DynEoMT: Learning Object Dynamicity from Online Segmentation Queries
papers.tldr: DynEoMT augments online video segmentation with per-region dynamic/static predictions using only current-frame inputs and propagated queries.

papers.abstract: Medical vision-language models (VLMs) allow a single model to perform clinical image analysis tasks ranging from diagnosis classification to report generation. However, joint adaptation is challenged by heterogeneous output formats, conflicting task gradients, and imbalanced training data. Hence, we present \textbf{Two-Stage Mixture-of-LoRA}, a framework built on MedGemma-1.5-4B. The framework uses a shared-specific Mixture-of-LoRA architecture comprising one shared LoRA and six task-specific expert LoRAs, together with a two-stage training procedure. In Stage 1, we jointly train the shared LoRA and all task-specific expert LoRAs on all tasks. In Stage 2, we first freeze the backbone, the shared LoRA, and all non-target experts, and refine one task expert at a time. Classification and regression then receive an additional modality-balanced continuation, in which smaller modality groups are repeated to match the largest group. In the FLARE 2026 Task 3 test sets, the proposed method achieves 0.85 balanced accuracy for classification, 0.48 micro-F1 for multi-label classification, 0.79 detection F1, and 17.39 regression MAE. Code is available at https://github.com/YuanYL03/MICCAI-FLARE-2026-Challenge-Task3-2D.
bullets: Addresses heterogeneous outputs, conflicting task gradients, and imbalanced data in joint medical VLM adaptation.
Uses one shared LoRA plus six task-specific expert LoRAs.
Jointly trains all adapters, then separately refines each task expert while freezing the others.
Adds modality-balanced continuation training for classification and regression.
On FLARE 2026 Task 3 test sets, reports 0.85 balanced accuracy, 0.48 micro-F1, 0.79 detection F1, and 17.39 regression MAE across task types.
papers.selection_reason: Multi-task medical vision-language model adaptation via Mixture-of-LoRA; fits multimodal LLM adaptation.
papers.title: Two-Stage Mixture-of-LoRA for Multi-Task Medical Vision-Language Learning
papers.tldr: Two-Stage Mixture-of-LoRA adapts MedGemma-1.5-4B to diverse medical vision-language tasks using shared and task-specific LoRA experts refined in two stages.
